title: Jatayu's last fight
hookLine: an old vulture king fights Ravana's chariot, loses, and is honored like a father
carry: nishkama karma: do right, leave the fruit
tomorrow: Rama runs home. what does he find at the hut?
last: THE GUEST IS GOD. THE LINE HOLDS.

cards: Sita steps out to give the wandering holy man his food. An ordinary kindness: a guest at the door, a bowl of rice. And the holy man changes.
The orange robe is gone, and a king stands in the clearing, ten heads, twenty arms, tall as a tree. Ravana. He tells her who he is and what he wants, and when she refuses, he takes her.
He lifts her into his chariot, and the chariot rises off the ground. Sita screams for Rama, for Lakshmana. She calls to the trees, the river, the deer, asking them to tell Rama where she's gone.

teach.b: His name is Jatayu. Valmiki calls him a king of the vultures, very old, and a friend of Rama's father; some tellings make him an eagle. He sees the chariot and does the math.
Ravana is young, armed, a king of demons. Jatayu is ancient. He goes anyway.
First he talks: put her down; a king shouldn't do what he'd punish in others. Ravana doesn't stop.
So the old bird attacks, and in Valmiki's telling he smashes the chariot, kills the donkeys that pull it, breaks Ravana's bow.

teach.h: FOR A FEW MINUTES, HE'S WINNING.
teach.b: For a few minutes, he's winning.

Then Ravana draws a sword and cuts off his wings. Jatayu falls, and Ravana flies south toward Lanka. On the way Sita drops her jewelry, wrapped in her cloth, onto a hilltop where some monkeys are watching.
Hold onto that. Jatayu holds on long enough to tell Rama which way she went. By any scoreboard, he failed.

teach.h: RAMA HONORS HIM LIKE A FATHER.
teach.b: Rama performs his funeral rites himself, the way a son would for a father.

teach.h: NISHKAMA KARMA: DO RIGHT, LEAVE THE FRUIT.
teach.b: Remember Krishna's line from day twenty-one: your right is to the action, never to its fruit. Hindus call that nishkama karma, action without grabbing at the result.
Many teachers point to Jatayu as that teaching with feathers: he did what was right because it was right, not because he could win.
When you stand up for someone and it doesn't work, the tradition doesn't count the result. It counts the dharma.

how: Hindus hear the story of Sita's abduction in Ramayana readings and in the Ramlila plays staged across north India before Dussehra; Jatayu is honored for giving his life for Sita, places in India are pointed to as where he fell, and teachers often hold him up as action without attachment to the result.

games.q: match the story to the teaching.
p: fought the chariot and lost his wings
dropped her jewelry as a trail
did Jatayu's funeral rites like a son
acting without grabbing at the result

s: Jatayu is a hero because he saved Sita
he didn't save her. he's honored for doing what was right without counting on winning.
for a while, Jatayu was winning
in Valmiki he smashes the chariot and breaks Ravana's bow before his wings are cut.
Jatayu died before anyone found him
he held on long enough to tell Rama which way Ravana went.

games.q: a kid is being mocked in your group chat. you speak up, and it doesn't stop anything. was it worth it? what fits Jatayu's teaching?
o: no. it only counts if it works.
yes. you did your part; the result was never yours to own.
only if someone noticed you did it.
games.why: nishkama karma: your right is to the action, not its fruit. Rama honored the bird who lost.

practice: Rama offered water at the river for Jatayu. Hindus still remember those they owe with water, a lamp, or simply their name.

Think of someone who stood up for you and lost: a parent who argued with a school and didn't win, a friend who got talked over. Say their name, light a lamp if you have one, and thank them for the doing, not the result.

wordCard.voice: The abduction. Sita carried off in Ravana's flying chariot, and an old bird who threw everything he had at it.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the name of the old vulture king, Jatayu, whom many tellings call an eagle.

carryVoice: Keep this one: nishkama karma. Do right, and leave the fruit. An old bird who lost still counts. Until tomorrow.
